findings.quote: The rule takes no noise rate and no clean data.
Under symmetric noise, a flipped label conflicts with the class structure that the other folds learn, so the out-of-fold model predicts against it far more often than against a clean label.
findings.fix: Present as the motivating argument ('we expect') and point to the recall and precision results as the evidence; the mechanism itself is not tested, and the claim holds for symmetric noise only.

findings.quote: The evidence supports the claim in every noisy setting we ran.
Most dropped samples are truly mislabeled (precision pooled over noisy runs is $71.3$\%\src{precision_pooled_noisy}), and most flipped labels are dropped.
The refit model beats plain logistic regression in all but one paired noisy run, and the MLP in every one, for symmetric noise up to $40$\%\src{noise_high_pct}.
On clean labels it costs a fraction of a point.
We show that the samples a cross-validated logistic regression disagrees with are mostly truly mislabeled, and that most flipped labels are among them, in every noisy setting we ran.
We present the drop-and-refit filter and show that it beats plain logistic regression and an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels under symmetric noise.
findings.fix: Restrict to where it is significant: it beats logistic regression on digits at 20% and 40% noise and on breast cancer at 40% noise (not significant on breast cancer at 20%, p = 0.12), and it beats the untuned MLP in all four noisy cells.

findings.quote: We report where it does not help: a small clean-label cost, a tie with the MLP on clean data, an unstable high-noise cell, about five times the fit time, and a scope of two small datasets and symmetric noise.
Our filter changes neither the loss nor the model and needs no noise model.
We add a checkable measurement of its precision, recall, accuracy gain and clean-label cost, not a new filtering idea. We do not compare against confident learning.
The rule has no threshold, uses no noise rate and holds out no clean data. It costs $K+1$ fits.
A flipped label contradicts that structure, so the out-of-fold model tends to predict the true class and the sample is dropped.
findings.fix: Keep the following 'argument, not a guarantee' caveat adjacent, and state that recall (79 to 98%) is the measured evidence; no experiment tests the mechanism.
